# roadmap-it

For work too big or too foggy for one plan (lane L). Each slice is built
through the normal flow as an S or M item. Unlike a plan, the roadmap is kept
in the repo's roadmap directory (default `docs/roadmap/<slug>.md`).

## Modes

| Invocation | Does |
|------------|------|
| `/roadmap-it "<idea>"` | Chart a new roadmap (§1-§5) |
| `/roadmap-it <file> next` | Show where every slice stands and start the next one (§6) |
| `/roadmap-it <file> replan` | Re-plan after slices ship or facts change (§7) |

## 1. Destination first

Call the Skill tool with "grill-it" to pin down the destination: what is
true when this effort is done, for whom, and what it is not. Write it as a
short statement plus numbered requirements (`G1`, `G2`, ...), each one
checkable. Call the Skill tool with "name-it" for the terms it introduces.
The destination fixes the scope; everything else follows from it.

## 2. See the ground

- Existing code: read `docs/reference/` if mapped, else call the Skill tool
  with "map-it" in chat mode. A risky area's health: "sweep-it".
- External facts the effort depends on: one subagent per question, on the
  mid-tier model, each calling the Skill tool with "look-it-up", in parallel, each reply
  `done`, `blocked` or `failed` plus one line, under 100 words.
- A new project: the greenfield agenda in
  [GREENFIELD.md](../scope-it/GREENFIELD.md) shapes the first milestone.

## 3. Slice

Grill breadth-first across the whole destination, then cut slices per
[SLICING.md](SLICING.md): vertical, shippable, lane S or M, each with what it
delivers, covers, is blocked by, and the check that verifies it. What cannot
be cut yet goes to Open decisions (sharp) or Fog (not yet sharp). Decisions
that are hard to reverse get an ADR through name-it. For a `--complete`
run, settle every decision now: [SWEEP.md](SWEEP.md).

## 4. Sequence

Group slices into milestones, each ending in something a user or operator can
see. Order by blocks, then risk (spikes and risky slices early), then value.
The first milestone proves the path end to end.

## 5. Check, write, approve

Write the roadmap per [FORMAT.md](FORMAT.md), then run the checks in
[SLICING.md](SLICING.md) (coverage of every `G`, no cycles, exit checks,
slice sizes) and fix what fails before showing it.

Present the destination, the milestones with their slices, the open decisions
and the out-of-scope list; end the turn. On approval record the date in the
file. With `--publish` or `DO_IT_PUBLISH_PLANS=true`, call the Skill tool
with "track-it" and publish one parent per milestone with a child per slice;
record each milestone ref in the frontmatter and each slice ref in its row's
`Ref` cell, so ship-it closes the slice's own issue.

## 6. Next

`work.mjs roadmap <file>` (the work-item script, [STATE.md](../do-it/STATE.md))
derives each slice's state, none stored: shipped or dropped (Status says
so); stale (a plan names it but git tracks the plan, so it was committed
outside ship-it: ask whether to mark it shipped or re-scope); in flight (a
plan names it); blocked (a Blocked-by slice not shipped, or a decision still
under Open decisions); refine; ready.

Show the slices by state, each with its `unmet` Verify clause. `blocking` lists
each open decision with the slices it blocks. Ask each before starting a slice:
call the Skill tool with "grill-it", one question with a recommended answer. A
settled one leaves Open decisions, gets a dated `Decisions so far` line, and is
reread. `next` is the first ready or refine slice by milestone, then risk (high
first), fewest blocks, id; offer a spike that blocks more slices instead. Start
it by reading [do-it](../do-it/SKILL.md) with `<file>#<id>`. A `refine` slice
gets a short grill first, then its Status is cleared.

## 7. Replan

After a slice ships, a spike or decision answers, or the destination moves:
1. Name the change and whether the destination moved or only the route.
2. Rewrite only slices that have not started; never touch shipped ones.
3. Turn sharp fog into slices or decisions; drop slices the shipped work made
   unnecessary (`dropped <date>: <why>`); re-cut any that grew past lane M.
4. Re-run the §5 checks, add a dated line to Decisions so far and to Changes,
   and show the diff for approval. A roadmap that already has `## Shipped`
   keeps it: the new line goes in a `## Changes` section after it (the first
   dated line creates one), never in a second Changes beside an existing one.
   Leave `completed:` as the owner set it.

## Rules

- No code here: the roadmap decides what and in which order; scope-it decides
  how. Each slice is at most lane M.
- ship-it finalizes a finished roadmap ([FINALIZE.md](../ship-it/FINALIZE.md)).

# scope-it

Read-only for code. Produces the plan and its state block
([STATE.md](../do-it/STATE.md)), then stops for approval.

## 1. Inputs

- An issue ref or path: fetch it with the `track-it` skill and list it under
  `sources:`. Several issues can feed one plan; merge overlapping ones.
- Free text: plan from it directly.
- A roadmap slice: its Delivers is the goal, its Verify becomes the plan's
  done-when, its Covers names the requirements to satisfy; it is recorded as
  `roadmap: <file>#<id>` (§3), and its `Ref` cell, if any, as `tracker`, so
  build-it starts and ship-it closes it. A slice bigger than lane M goes back to
  `/roadmap-it <file> replan`.
- The lane from `do-it`, else size it with [LANES.md](../do-it/LANES.md).
- A run record exists (full or ultra): [NONINTERACTIVE.md](NONINTERACTIVE.md), no grill.

## 2. Grill, scaled to the lane

| Lane | Grill |
|------|-------|
| S | 0-3 questions in one turn, each with a recommended answer. Zero when the issue already has acceptance criteria and the code answers the rest. |
| M | Call the Skill tool with "grill-it", then with "name-it". Add the agenda in [GRILL.md](GRILL.md). End the turn after each round. |

A new project (no source yet) adds [GREENFIELD.md](GREENFIELD.md) at either lane.

Find facts yourself (code, ADRs, the area's context per it-core,
`docs/reference/`); ask only for decisions. A library, API or standard fact
the code does not settle: call the Skill tool with "look-it-up". For seams,
call the Skill tool with "design-it" and use its vocabulary.

No `CONTEXT.md` for the plan's area: never write one while scouting; propose
"create `<area>/CONTEXT.md` with `/map-it <area>`" as a step at approval (§5).

## 3. Write the plan

Create the plan file with `work.mjs new <id> --lane s|m --title "<title>" --brief`
(the work-item script, [STATE.md](../do-it/STATE.md)); it writes the full
state block, `status: draft`. Then fill the block with `work.mjs set`:
`sources`, `phases` (lane M), `assumptions`, and `roadmap` or `todo` when
the input carried one. Write the body per [PLAN-FORMAT.md](PLAN-FORMAT.md):

- Lane S: below the block in `docs/planning/<id>.md`.
- Lane M: below it in `docs/planning/<id>/README.md`, plus a `phase-N.md` each.

Every step or phase states how it is verified (`step → verify: check`). A slice that
compares or measures adds a last step ([PLAN-FORMAT.md](PLAN-FORMAT.md)).
Risk-area lane S, or top-tier: [PLANNER.md](PLANNER.md).

Then run the two passes in [CHECKS.md](CHECKS.md) before showing anything:
an analyze pass (coverage both ways, verify checks, names, blocks, rules)
and a builder check (a fresh `it-reviewer` agent reads only the plan and
returns the questions a builder would ask). Fix the plan from both; questions
only the user can answer join the approval turn.

## 4. ADR only when warranted

Write an ADR only for a decision that is hard to reverse, surprising without
context, and the result of a real trade-off; otherwise it lives in the plan.
Follow [name-it's ADR format](../name-it/ADR-FORMAT.md), status `Proposed`,
next free number in the repo's ADR directory, linked from the plan.

## 5. Approve

Present the plan in chat: the steps or phases (`Blocked by`, what each delivers),
the `/map-it <area>` context step when §2 proposed it, the assumptions, and any
builder-check questions (each with a recommended answer). The plan stays `draft`.
End the turn; lane M makes this its last grill round ([GRILL.md](GRILL.md)).

On approval, `work.mjs event <id> approve --brief`. Edits the user asks for are made
and re-presented; approval of the edited plan counts.

## 6. Publish (optional)

With `--publish`, or when the tracker config sets `DO_IT_PUBLISH_PLANS=true`,
call the Skill tool with "track-it" and run `publish` for the plan. For Jira,
settle the spec's `project`, `components` and `parent` epic in the approval
turn (config values recommended; `none` when the user says not to). Record
the parent and per-phase refs it returns with `work.mjs set <id> tracker
'{"kind":"<kind>","ref":"<ref>","phases":{"1":"<ref>"}}'`. Lanes S and XS do
not publish by default.

## 7. Close

> Plan `<id>` approved: lane <lane>, <N> phase(s). **Next:** `/build-it <id>`.

When `do-it` called this skill, return `done` and let it continue.

## Rules

- No code edits, no commits. Out-of-scope work goes to `log-it`.
- Rejected ideas get one line under the plan's `## Non-goals`.

# setup-it

One-time onboarding for a repo. Safe to re-run: it shows what would change
and writes nothing that is already right.

## 1. Detect (never ask what you can read)

Read, without writing anything:

- **Project state:** new or existing, per the project-state table in
  [SCOUT.md](../do-it/SCOUT.md) §1. Existing and no `docs/reference/`: note
  it for §4.
- **Commands:** test, lint, format, type-check, from `package.json` scripts,
  `Makefile`, `pyproject.toml`, `build.gradle`/`pom.xml`, `Cargo.toml`, the CI
  workflow, and test scripts (`*.test.sh`, `test/`, `tests/`). Record `none`
  for a kind that does not exist. Pick a per-file lint command if the linter
  takes paths (for `DO_IT_LINT_CMD`, with `{file}`). They are recorded once,
  in the `AGENTS.md` `Commands:` line ([PROPOSAL.md](PROPOSAL.md) §4), which
  build-it and map-it read instead of rediscovering.
- **Current config:** `node <track-it dir>/scripts/tracker.mjs config` (the
  `track-it` skill's directory is `../track-it/`). It shows existing
  `.do-it/` values, the detected context, context map, changelog, ADR and
  reference paths, and warnings.
- **Tracker hints:** whether `origin` (not forks or upstreams) is GitHub,
  Jira keys in recent commit subjects, `JIRA_*` names in `.env.example`, an
  existing `docs/issues/`. `--tracker` overrides all of them.
- **Agent docs:** `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, whether either already has a
  do-it section, the repo's own writing rules (the appended text follows
  them), and any other workflow already defined there that uses
  `docs/issues/` or `docs/planning/` (flag the overlap in the proposal).
- **Protected branches:** `node <this skill's dir>/scripts/default-branch.mjs <repo root>`
  prints the remote's default branch and the `DO_IT_PROTECTED_BRANCHES` value to
  write; `write: false` means skip it.
- **Compliance:** `.compliance-rules/` and any `checks.json`.
- **OpenCode:** `node <this skill's dir>/scripts/opencode-check.mjs <repo root>`
  prints whether `external_directory` is safe; `applies: false` means skip it.

## 2. Propose (one turn, every item with a default)

Follow [PROPOSAL.md](PROPOSAL.md). Show each file as the exact text or diff
it would write, and mark items that are already correct as "no change".

## 3. Write on approval

Write only the items the user accepts, then re-run
`tracker.mjs config` and show the result. Any warning (a secret in the
committed file, a configured path that does not exist) is fixed before
closing.

## 4. Close

> Set up <repo>: <files written>. Tracker: <kind>. Lint: <command | none>.
> Skipped / Not checked / Risk.
> **Next:** `/map-it` (existing repo, no map), else `/do-it "<first change>"`.

## Rules

- Never write a secret anywhere in the repo. Tokens go in
  `~/.config/do-it/config.env` or `.do-it/local.env` (see the `track-it`
  skill's [CONFIG.md](../track-it/CONFIG.md)); say which keys the user needs
  to set there and let them do it.
- Append to `AGENTS.md`; never rewrite what is there.
- Re-running replaces only the do-it section and the `.do-it/config.env` keys
  it manages; everything else is left as found.

# ship-it

The only step that touches git history, and only on the user's word. Nothing
is written before the user answers the one question (§2).

## 1. Gate

`work.mjs` below is the work-item script in [STATE.md](../do-it/STATE.md);
a refused command (exit 1) is `blocked`.

- **Lane XS:** no state block, no id to close; [RESUME.md](RESUME.md).
  **`--roadmap <file>`:** [FINALIZE.md](FINALIZE.md).
- **Otherwise** `work.mjs show <id>` and require `status: shipping` and
  `audit.verdict: PASS`. First run: `work.mjs fingerprint <id>` must equal
  `audit.fingerprint`, else the code moved after the audit:
  `work.mjs event <id> reaudit`, stop, **Next:** `/prove-it <id>`.
- **Resumed after review** (`ship.prepared` set): [RESUME.md](RESUME.md).

## 2. The one question

One turn; write nothing yet. **Show** (information, no answer needed):

- `git status --short`: everything that will be in the change.
- The docs this will write, per [DOCS.md](DOCS.md): ADRs to accept, the
  area's `CONTEXT.md` and map row, the changelog entry (lane XS: changelog
  only, when the repo keeps one), a risk-area rollback note.
- Tracker, to-do and roadmap updates: one `close` per ref (state block refs,
  the slice's `Ref` cell, or `--ref`) with a comment drawn from the changelog; a
  roadmap's last slice also shows what finalize offers a to e will write
  ([FINALIZE.md](FINALIZE.md)).
- Numbered: the audit's Should and Nice findings (no changelog), surfaced
  `defects:`, a roadmap Verify clause they leave unmet ([DOCS.md](DOCS.md)).
- Guardrail candidates or a failed audit round: one line offering `/retro-it <id>`;
  `work.mjs close` deletes the candidates, so it runs before "commit now".
- The commit message: `<id>: <summary>` (the commit id, it-core Git), a
  blank line, one bullet per phase or step; on a protected branch (`main`,
  `master`, `DO_IT_PROTECTED_BRANCHES`), the feature branch to create first.

**Ask** at most three things, numbered, each left out when empty; an answer
to the last alone keeps the defaults:

1. `assumptions:`, numbered: reject any? (default: keep all). Lane XS, no id: [RESUME.md](RESUME.md).
2. To log, and to finalize: new `shortcut:` markers with no upgrade trigger, the
   audit findings and surfaced defects above (default: findings and defects, no
   markers); a roadmap's last slice adds finalize offers a to e
   ([FINALIZE.md](FINALIZE.md)), every one taken by default
3. **Commit now** (say "do it") or **leave it for review**? Recommend leave it
   unless the user asked to commit; `DO_IT_COMMIT=never` makes it the only option.

## 3. After the answer

1. **A rejected assumption that changes code:** `work.mjs event <id>
   reject-assumption <n> "<instead>"`; stop. **Next:** `/do-it <id>`. One
   that changes nothing: `work.mjs set` the assumptions.
2. **Docs and closes, before any commit:** write what §2 showed per
   [DOCS.md](DOCS.md), updating an earlier run's; park or file the markers; log
   the chosen findings (no changelog), the finalize offers taken
   ([FINALIZE.md](FINALIZE.md)). Then close all that lives in the repo, so one
   commit holds it all (a user commit after review included):
   - the refs to close: `todo`, `roadmap` and `tracker` from
     `work.mjs show <id>`; lane XS: `--todo` and `--ref`;
   - each roadmap slice: Status `shipped <date> <work id>` (unmet Verify: DOCS.md),
     a dated line in its Changes (the first dated line creates `## Changes`);
     each to-do id: call the Skill tool with "log-it"
     to mark it done with the work id (lane XS: the commit);
   - a local-tracker ref: `tracker.mjs close <ref>`, deleting the issue file
     (already gone: an earlier run closed it);
   - `event <id> ship-prepared` (not lane XS; its no-id case is in
     [RESUME.md](RESUME.md)).
3. **Leave it for review:** stop; the plan stays (`status: shipping`), the
   remote tracker stays open. Repeat the commit message and the command that
   finishes, `/ship-it <id>` (lane XS: `--lane xs` with its `--ref` and
   `--todo`), which commits, or finishes once the user has committed.
4. **Commit now** (or a resumed run after the user committed). Step 2 has
   already run, so the working tree holds the whole change:
   - create the feature branch if §2 named one; stage by path (never
     `git add -A`), with the issue, to-do and roadmap edits from step 2; commit
     with the approved message (already committed by the user: nothing to stage);
   - only after the commit succeeds: `work.mjs close <id>` (lane XS: none),
     then the remote tracker (GitHub, Jira) closes with a comment drawn from
     the changelog; it cannot be part of the commit, and a tracker failure
     never undoes the commit.

## 4. Close

"Shipped <id>: committed as abc123 | prepared, left for review", then
Skipped / Not checked / Risk, then **Next:** (the finish command, push when
ready, or nothing). On a roadmap slice, the slash command for the next one, never a script.

## Rules

- Never commit, push, amend or squash without an explicit "do it" in this run;
  push or open a PR only when the user asks.
- A run record exists for the item: [RUNMODE.md](RUNMODE.md) replaces §2's question.
- One commit for code and docs together unless the user asks for two; hooks
  still run on it, and a compliance block stops it.

# sketch-it

A sketch is code written to be thrown away. It exists to answer one question,
and its only lasting output is the answer.

## 1. Name the question

Write the question as one sentence before any code: "Can an order be
refunded after a partial shipment without double-counting stock?" A sketch
without a written question drifts into a prototype of everything.

Then pick the branch:

| The question is about | Branch |
|-----------------------|--------|
| Behaviour: states, transitions, rules, data shape, an API's feel | [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md): one HTML file that drives a pure model with buttons |
| Appearance: layout, hierarchy, what a screen should show | [UI.md](UI.md): two to five structurally different variants on one route |

Unsure which: the area decides. A service or domain module points to logic; a
page or component points to UI. Record the choice as an assumption in the
sketch's header and carry on.

## 2. Ground rules

- **Labelled as a sketch.** Place it beside the code it informs and put
  `sketch` in its file or route name, so nobody mistakes it for product code.
- **One command or one double-click to run.** Nothing to configure.
- **Memory only.** No real database, queue or external call unless the
  question is about that very thing; then use a scratch store named so it is
  obviously disposable.
- **No polish.** No tests, no error handling beyond what keeps it running, no
  abstractions. Speed of learning is the point.
- **State on screen.** After every action or variant switch, show the state
  that matters, so the person driving it sees cause and effect.
- **Uncommitted.** Per `it-core`, the sketch stays in the working tree; it is
  never part of a do-it commit.

## 3. Hand it over

Give the user the file path or URL and the variant keys. The useful moments
are surprises: "that should not be allowed", "I want the header from B with
the list from C". Adjust the sketch when they ask; it is cheap.

## 4. Record the answer, then remove the sketch

The answer outlives the sketch; the sketch does not.

1. Write the verdict: the question, what was tried, what was decided and why.
   - Inside a do-it work item: add it to the plan's `## Decisions` (it is an
     approved decision for `scope-it`).
   - A domain term or a hard-to-reverse choice came out of it: call the Skill
     tool with "name-it" for the term in the area's `CONTEXT.md` or an ADR.
   - Neither: put the verdict in the closing message.
2. Keep what proved itself, rewritten properly: a pure logic module can move
   into the real code with tests; a winning layout is rebuilt in the real
   page, not promoted from the sketch.
3. Delete the sketch files and any sketch route, and say so. If the user
   wants it kept for reference, move it to a clearly named scratch location
   outside the shipped code and name that path.

# Skill mechanics

What changes when the document is a skill. The writing guidance in
[SKILL.md](SKILL.md) still applies; this repo's own rules are in its
`AGENTS.md` and are enforced by `npm run check`.

## Typed or automatic

| | Automatic (model-invoked) | Typed (user-invoked) |
|---|---|---|
| Frontmatter | no `disable-model-invocation` | `disable-model-invocation: true` |
| Description | what it does, then "Use when ..." with the distinct triggers | one line for a human reading a command list |
| Who can start it | the agent on its own, another skill, or the user | only the user, by typing it |
| Context cost | its description, every turn | none |

Never summarize the process in a description: an agent that reads a summary
may follow it instead of the skill. Choose automatic only when the agent or
another skill must reach the skill without the user. A step the user drives (the do-it flow steps, deepen-it,
pass-it) is typed.

A skill calls an automatic skill as Call the Skill tool with "<name>", with
the name in quotes so `npm run check` can verify it. A typed skill cannot be
loaded that way (the host refuses), so another skill reaches it by reading
its file: "read [scope-it](../scope-it/SKILL.md) and follow it".

## Files

- One directory per skill directly under `skills/`, named after the skill;
  the frontmatter `name` matches the directory.
- `SKILL.md` stays within 100 lines (150 is a hard error). Detail goes in
  sibling files one level deep, linked from the step that needs them.
- Links between skills stay inside `skills/` (`../do-it/STATE.md`), so they
  work after a symlink install. Scripts a skill runs live in its own
  `scripts/` directory and are referenced from the skill's directory.
- Shared conventions have one home (`do-it/STATE.md`, `do-it/LANES.md`);
  other skills link there instead of restating them.

## Subagents

A subagent inherits the model of the session that starts it, which is the
top tier for most users. The role agents in `agents/` pin their own model and
tools, so a skill names the agent and the tier follows:

| Agent | Tier | Does |
|-------|------|------|
| `it-scout` | cheap | read-only exploring and mapping |
| `it-reviewer` | mid | review one diff against one source, validate a finding, read a plan as its builder |
| `it-builder` | mid | build one plan phase, in a worktree or in place |
| `it-planner` | top | draft a plan |
| `it-skeptic` | top | try to prove one claim false |

Installed as the plugin, an agent's name carries the plugin prefix
(`do-it:it-reviewer`) and the Agent tool refuses the bare name; installed by
symlink it is bare. Start it by the name the Agent tool lists.

Every paragraph that starts a subagent names one of these agents or a tier:
**cheap tier** (`model: haiku` in Claude Code), **mid-tier model**
(`model: sonnet`), or **session model** for work whose quality is the point,
with the reason. A host without the agents (OpenCode, or an install that
skipped them) starts a general-purpose subagent on that tier instead. A task
that needs tools an agent withholds, such as web search for `look-it-up`,
names the tier and not an agent.

A foreground call blocks the parent until the agent finishes. In OpenCode 2
that looks like a hung session, and the TUI shows nothing to act on. There the
tool is `subagent`: pass `background: true` for an agent a skill says runs in
the background, and for every agent of a parallel batch. The call returns at
once and the host reports the result when the child finishes; do not poll or
sleep. Foreground stays right when the next step needs the report and nothing
else can run meanwhile.

Write the delegation as the tool call ("Call the Agent tool with `it-scout`"),
not "hands off to" or "a subagent checks": a softer line was read and skipped
in a headless run.

Give a subagent pointers, never the conversation, and a word cap on its
report: the parent re-reads the report on every later turn.
`npm run check` fails a paragraph that starts a subagent and names no tier or
no word cap.

Only the main context fans out. A skill that itself runs inside a subagent
does its sub-steps inline and starts no further subagents: the parent could
not cap, read or pay for a second layer. Every agent carries the voice rules
of `skills/it-core/VOICE.md` and a `## Report` contract with its cap;
`npm run gen` keeps the copies current.

## Names

Skill names are short `-it` verbs (`scope-it`, `track-it`) so they never
collide with another skill set installed beside this one. Before adding a
name, check it against the other skill repos in use and against the host's
built-in commands.

## When to split off a skill

Split when a part has its own trigger the agent should react to on its own,
or when another skill needs to reach it. Each new automatic skill adds a
description to every turn, so the independent reach has to be worth that.
When typed skills multiply, one typed entry that names the others (as do-it
does for the flow) keeps the list a person must remember short.

## Before handing off

```bash
npm test && npm run check
```

name: skill-it
description: Write or revise a skill, an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or any document an agent follows, so it runs the same way every time and stays small. Use when creating or editing a skill, changing agent instruction files, splitting a skill that grew too long, or reviewing why an agent skipped or misread instructions.

# skill-it

An agent document is a program written in prose: the aim is that every run
takes the same path, not that every run says the same words. For skill files
specifically (frontmatter, invocation, naming, the checks this repo runs),
read [SKILL-MECHANICS.md](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) as well.

## Pointers decide when material is read

Anything an agent reaches from elsewhere is reached through a **pointer**: a
skill's description, a line in `AGENTS.md`, a link inside a skill. The
wording of the pointer, not the quality of what it points at, decides whether
the agent goes there. When material that matters keeps being skipped, sharpen
its pointer before inlining the material.

A good pointer says what the material is and lists the distinct situations
that should send the agent to it, one phrase per situation. Synonyms for one
situation are one situation; keep one. Pointers that are always loaded
(descriptions, `AGENTS.md`) cost tokens on every turn, so they are pruned
hardest.

## Two budgets

- **Context:** what sits in the agent's window every turn whether it is used
  or not. Descriptions and always-loaded files spend it.
- **Attention of the person:** what the human must remember exists. Typed
  commands spend it. Spend it where a human should choose, save it elsewhere.

## Layout of a document

Two kinds of content: **steps** (what to do, in order) and **reference**
(rules and facts looked up when needed). Place each by how soon it is needed:

1. Steps the agent always takes: in the main file, in order.
2. Reference most runs need: in the main file, grouped by topic, with each
   topic's definition, rules and exceptions together under one heading.
3. Reference only some paths need: a sibling file, linked from the step that
   needs it, with the link saying when to read it.

Inline what every path needs; move behind a link what only some paths reach.
A file can be too long even when every line is live: past the budget, split
by path or by stage rather than trimming useful lines.

## Every step ends on a check

Each step finishes on a condition the agent can test: "every caller listed
with its path", not "understand the callers". A vague end invites stopping
early, especially when the next steps are visible. Sharpen the condition
first; split the later steps into another file or subagent only if a sharp
condition still gets rushed. The demand in the wording sets the effort:
"every rule applied to every changed file" asks for more than "check the
rules".

## Words that carry weight

Prefer a short word the model already knows well (tight, red, frontier,
seam, fog) over a sentence describing the same idea, and reuse that exact
word everywhere the idea appears. It saves tokens and gives the agent one
handle to think with. Use a term the project already uses in its code and
prompts when one exists; coin a new one only with a definition.

Say what to do, not what to avoid: "write one-line comments" works better
than a ban, because naming the unwanted behaviour makes it more likely. Keep
a prohibition only as a hard guardrail, paired with the positive target.

## Keep it lean

- **One home per rule.** Repeating a rule in two files costs tokens, drifts,
  and makes it look more important than it is. Link to the home instead.
- **Do not copy the environment.** `package.json` scripts, config files and
  `--help` output are already the truth; restating them goes stale. Write down
  what the repo cannot tell the agent: the reason, the convention, the trap.
- **Delete no-ops.** A sentence the model would follow anyway changes
  nothing. Test a doubtful one by running the document without it. Remove
  whole sentences rather than trimming words.
- **Prune for staleness.** Every edit is a chance to remove a line that no
  longer bears on the task.

# sweep-it

Read-only for code. Audits what is already there, unlike `prove-it`, which
audits one change. Reports; changes nothing; files only what the user picks.

## 1. Scope

| Invocation | Scope |
|------------|-------|
| `/sweep-it` | The whole repo, deepest where a mistake costs most |
| `/sweep-it <path>` | That path and what it calls |
| `/sweep-it --hot` | Files changed most in recent history (`git log --format= --name-only -n 300 \| sort \| uniq -c \| sort -rn`) |

Start from `docs/reference/` when it exists; otherwise read the README,
build and deploy config, dependency manifests, entry points and tests. Find
the expected load (one user running a script, or many users at once) and say
which you assumed. Read the risky paths end to end: user input, auth, money,
data writes, background jobs, shared state.

## 2. Lenses

Run the lenses in [LENSES.md](LENSES.md): bugs, risk, scale, test gaps, debt,
drift, lean, and a short architecture pass. A repo-wide sweep on a host with
subagents: one fresh-context `it-reviewer` agent (mid-tier model) per group of
lenses (correctness and risk; tests; debt, drift and lean), each reporting
in its `## Report` shape under 500 words and given the scope, the assumed load and
[LENSES.md](LENSES.md); merge their findings here and re-check each one.

Compliance: call the Skill tool with "guard-it" on the scope, so repo
rules and the mechanical checks are applied the same way as in `prove-it`.

## 3. Check before reporting

The finding contract in [REPORT.md](../prove-it/REPORT.md) applies: a concrete
case or no finding; recorded decisions (ADRs, `shortcut:` markers that name
their limit) are not findings; before calling code unused, grep the whole
tree including tests, config and string references. Prefer fixes that delete
code. At most 20 findings; say how many smaller ones were left out. Validate
every Must per [VALIDATE.md](../prove-it/VALIDATE.md) before reporting it;
rejected ones go under Not confirmed with the reason.

## 4. Report

Shape in [REPORT.md](REPORT.md). Written to
`docs/reference-audit/<date>-<scope>.md`, or in chat only with `--chat` (the
default when a model-invoked run was a quick question). Present the findings
and the verdict in chat either way.

## 5. File what matters

Ask once which numbered findings to file, and where. Must and Should go to
an issue: call the Skill tool with "log-it" (`kind: issue`, `source: sweep-it`, the
finding's case and fix in the body). Nice findings default to the to-do list:
call the Skill tool with "log-it" (`kind: todo`, tag `nice-to-have`, the
finding's location as source). Never file the whole report unasked.

> Swept <scope>: <N> findings (<M> Must). Filed: <refs or none>.
> **Next:** `/do-it <ref>` for a filed issue, or
> `/deepen-it <area>` for the structural notes.

Not checked: the parts not read, commands not run, the load assumed.

name: test-it
description: Build behaviour test-first, one failing test at a time, at agreed test seams, with tests that survive refactoring. Use when building a feature or fixing a bug test-first, when the user mentions TDD or red-green, or when asked to add integration or regression tests.

# test-it

Red, then green, one thin slice at a time. The aim is not coverage: it is a
small set of tests that pin down what the code promises and keep passing
while its insides change.

Name tests and fixtures in the project's own domain words (the Terms in the
area's `CONTEXT.md`, per it-core), and stay inside the decisions its ADRs record.

## Where the tests sit

Tests go through a module's interface at a seam, in the sense
[design-it](../design-it/SKILL.md) defines (the place where an interface sits
and behaviour can be swapped), and nowhere deeper.

- **Seams already agreed** (`build-it` passes the plan's `## Seams`): test at
  exactly those. Do not ask the user to confirm them again.
- **No agreed seams** (a standalone run): propose them before the first test,
  each with one line on what a test there catches and what it lets through.
  Confirm once, then go. Agreeing seams first is what puts the effort on
  risky logic instead of on every trivial path.
- **The seam itself looks wrong** (too shallow, leaking internals, nowhere
  natural to put it): call the Skill tool with "design-it" for the module and
  interface vocabulary, and settle the shape before writing tests.

## The loop

1. Pick the next behaviour, the thinnest one that teaches you something.
2. Write one test at a seam that fails for the right reason. Run it; see the
   failure message you expected.
3. Write the least code that turns it green. Nothing for the test after next.
4. Run the whole relevant suite, then go back to 1.

Each slice cuts through every layer it needs (a tracer bullet), so the next
test is chosen with what the last one taught you. Writing every test up
front and then all the code locks in a guess about the design before the
code has had a say.

Cleaning up structure is not a step in this loop. Note it and leave it for
review (`review-it`) or a separate change.

## A keeper test

- Exercises behaviour a caller can observe, through the seam.
- Reads as a statement of fact about the system ("an expired coupon is
  refused at checkout"), not a description of the code path.
- Gets its expected value from somewhere independent of the code: a literal,
  a worked example, the spec. Never recompute the answer the way the code
  does.
- Breaks when behaviour breaks, and only then.

[tests.md](tests.md) shows keepers next to the usual failures.
[mocking.md](mocking.md) covers what to fake, and how to shape a boundary so
faking it is easy.

## Smells that mean start the test again

- It fails after a refactor that changed no behaviour.
- It mocks a module you own, asserts call order, or reaches a private member.
- It checks the result through a side door (reads the table directly) instead
  of through the interface that promised it.
- It cannot fail, because it asserts what the code computes by the same
  method.

# track-it

One interface, three trackers. Other skills call this one; none of them talks
to GitHub or Jira directly.

## Pick the route

1. **An MCP tool for that tracker is in your tool list** (a Jira or GitHub
   connector): use it for the operation. It carries the user's own auth.
2. **Otherwise**, the CLI beside this file:

   ```bash
   node <this skill's dir>/scripts/tracker.mjs <command> ...
   ```

Both routes do the same operations; results go into the work item's state
block the same way.

## Operations

| Command | Does | Local | GitHub (`gh`) | Jira (REST v2) |
|---------|------|-------|---------------|----------------|
| `config` | Effective config, secrets redacted, with the file each value came from, and `untrusted` keys | | | |
| `trust` | Pins the repo's current `DO_IT_LINT_CMD` / `JIRA_BASE_URL` values for this user ([CONFIG.md](CONFIG.md#trust)). Run it only when the user says to, after showing them the values | | | |
| `create --title T --type bug\|feature\|todo\|defer --body-file F` | New issue | `docs/issues/<slug>.md` | `gh issue create` | Task (Bug for `bug`); also `--project`, `--component` (repeatable) and `--epic` or `--parent` (a sub-task), each refused when unset and not `none` |
| `list [--status open\|closed\|all]` | Issues, open by default | reads `docs/issues/` | local only, plus a note | local only, plus a note |
| `get <ref>` | Title, status, body, comments | reads the file | `gh issue view` | issue + comments |
| `comment <ref> --body-file F` | Add a comment | appends to `## Log` | `gh issue comment` | comment (wiki markup) |
| `start <ref>` | Work began | `status: in-progress` | adds `DO_IT_GITHUB_START_LABEL` if set | assigns `JIRA_ASSIGNEE` if unassigned, transition `JIRA_START_TRANSITION` |
| `close <ref> --body-file F` | Work shipped | deletes the file; git history keeps it | `gh issue close` | comment, transition `JIRA_DONE_TRANSITION` |
| `publish --spec F` | Parent + one child per phase | nothing | parent issue with a task list | Epic (or `JIRA_DEFAULT_EPIC`) + Tasks, all with the spec's `components` |

`publish` takes JSON: `{"title", "body", "phases": [{"n", "title", "body"}],
"parent"?, "components"?, "project"?}` (`parent: "none"` files the phases
with no epic). Write it to a temp file or pipe it with `--spec -`. The caller
records the returned `parent` and `phases` under `tracker:` in the state
block, through the work-item script ([STATE.md](../do-it/STATE.md)).
A `publish` that fails part way prints the refs it made with an `error` and
exits 1; record those refs, then finish the rest by hand.

A ref routes by its shape, whatever the default tracker is:
`docs/issues/x.md` is local; `owner/repo#42`, `#42`, `gh-42` or an issue URL
on any GitHub host is GitHub; `ABC-123` (any case) or a `/browse/ABC-123` URL
is Jira. GitHub results carry `owner/repo#N` (`host/owner/repo#N` on a
GitHub Enterprise host, passed to `gh` as `-R host/owner/repo`) so later calls
reach the same repo; use that form when recording refs. `create` and `publish` use
`DO_IT_TRACKER` unless `--tracker` says otherwise. When `gh` rejects a label,
the issue is still created and the result lists `labelsDropped`.

## Configuration

See [CONFIG.md](CONFIG.md). Run `tracker.mjs config` before the first remote
call in a session; act on its `warnings` (a secret in a committed file) and its `untrusted`
repo values (show them to the user and offer `trust`).

## Rules

- Bodies are Markdown; the Jira adapter converts them to wiki markup.
- Never print tokens. Never write secrets into `.do-it/config.env`.
- A tracker failure is reported in the closing message and never blocks
  building or shipping. Missing config: say which keys, point to CONFIG.md.
- Jira transitions are matched by name; when one is missing the CLI returns
  `skipped` with the available names. Report it; do not guess another.

# usage-it

Shows where tokens went: main sessions and subagents, by model and project,
over time. Read-only: it reads the ledger and writes one HTML file.

## The ledger

The `Stop` and `SubagentStop` hooks add one line per agent run to
`~/.claude/do-it/usage/<day>.jsonl` (override with `DO_IT_USAGE_DIR`). Raw
days are kept 30 days (`DO_IT_USAGE_DAYS`); older days roll up into
`rollup.jsonl`, one row per day, agent, model and project, kept 365 days
(`DO_IT_USAGE_ROLLUP_DAYS`). Tokens only, no dollar estimate: prices change.
The OpenCode plugin adds the same rows from its events (`scripts/opencode.mjs`).
`scripts/ledger.mjs` owns reading, writing and pruning; do not edit the files.

## 1. Fill the ledger if it is empty

The hooks write each run as it stops, and the report re-imports the last two days
itself, so a run in progress or on a host without the hooks is still counted.

Without hooks installed, or on a first run, the ledger has nothing. Run:

```bash
node <this skill's directory>/scripts/usage.mjs --import --days 30 --by agent
```

It backfills from the transcripts Claude Code already keeps and prints a
summary. Safe to repeat: a run is keyed by its id and replaced, never added
twice. Skip this step when the ledger already has recent days.

## 2. Build the report

```bash
node <this skill's directory>/scripts/report.mjs --days <N> --open
```

`N` is the user's range, default 30. For a range in hours, pass `--hours <N>`
instead (raw days only, so at most 30 days back). Past 60 days the charts group by month.
It prints the path of the file it wrote
(`~/.claude/do-it/reports/usage-<date>.html`); `--out <file>` writes elsewhere.
The page is self-contained: no network, light and dark themes.

## 3. Say what it shows

Give the path, then at most five lines taken from the page's "What stands out"
list and its tables (the top-sessions table shows the heaviest sessions by id, project and day): the largest consumer, whether main sessions ran on the
top model, unpinned agent types (no model of their own) on the top model, and the cache-read share.
The "Context outliers" table lists main sessions by peak context (start and peak
tokens, flagged above twice the median peak); a long peak, not a heavy start, is
what `/clear` and `pass-it` address. Quote numbers from the report; do not infer causes it does not show. Nothing
recorded for the range: say so and name the ledger directory.

## The plan meter

Claude Code caches its `/usage` percentages in `~/.claude.json`
(`cachedUsageUtilization`: the 5-hour and weekly windows, with reset times).
The `Stop` hook and the report copy a new reading into `snapshots.ndjson` in
the ledger directory, with this host's tokens since the week began, so the trend
builds up without typing. When the cached reading is over 10 minutes old, the report
and `usage.mjs --snapshot` first run `claude -p /usage` (a local command: no model
call, no tokens) to refresh it; `DO_IT_USAGE_REFRESH=0` turns that off. The hook
never does, since it would start a session of its own. The report's "Plan meter" section charts
the week, adds a per-day table and projects when the week would reach 100% (the
average pace since the reset, and the pace over the last 6 hours or more). The
numbers are account-wide, from any host; the tokens stored are this host's.

`usage.mjs --snapshot` takes the cached reading now and prints the pace. By hand
(when the cache is missing): `--snapshot --week <pct> --resets <ISO with offset>
[--session <pct>] [--at <ISO>]`. The field is not a documented interface; if
Claude Code changes it, readings stop and the section says so.

## The `/clear` nudge

When a main session's context first passes 300000 tokens, the `Stop` hook shows
the user one line suggesting `/pass-it`, then `/clear`. It never blocks and adds
nothing to the model's context. `DO_IT_CLEAR_AT` sets the size; `0` turns it off.

## Reading it

- Work tokens are input, output and cache writes. Cache reads are the context
  re-read each turn; they are cheap per token but dominate long sessions.
- `main` is the user's own session; every other row is a delegated agent run.
- A session's model is the one it used most; a session that switched models
  counts under the majority.
- Sessions of other repos appear too, under their project name.

`usage.mjs --baseline` prints what do-it adds to every session (the session-start
block, `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`, the invocable skill descriptions) beside the
median start context recorded. `usage.mjs --from <iso> --to <iso>` (or `--hours`)
limits any summary to the tokens in that window, so a step's usage is its start
and end time with `--by agent`.
A run straddling an edge is cut there by its 15-minute buckets, so an edge off a
quarter hour can move up to 7.5 minutes of tokens across it, and a window
shorter than 15 minutes counts the buckets it overlaps (two adjacent short
windows can both report one). The run counts once: in the window that holds its
first bucket, as 0 in the others. `--by day|month` groups a share by the run's
start day. A run without buckets counts whole by its last message, and the
output says so (`--json` rows carry `whole`, the runs counted whole in that row).

For a quick table instead of a page: `usage.mjs --days N --by agent|model|day|month|project`.

# do-it Agent skills for Claude Code and OpenCode that run one workflow from issue to ship, sized to the work: a typo gets three steps, an epic gets a roadmap. Always-on coding standards and compliance hooks come with it. ```text /do-it "rate-limit the login endpoint" → lane S: plan (one approval) → build → audit → ship (one question) ``` ## Quick start 1. [Install](#install) (Node 18+): one command links the skills, agents and hooks. 2. In a repo, run `/setup-it` once. It detects your test and lint commands, tracker and doc paths, and writes only what you accept. 3. Run `/do-it ""` or `/do-it `. It sizes the work and asks only when a decision is yours. Skills marked *typed* below run only when you type the slash command; the rest the model can also pick up from what you say. ## Why this exists Coding agents fail in a few predictable ways. Each step of the flow answers one. | What goes wrong | What do-it does about it | |-----------------|--------------------------| | A one-line fix gets a plan, a review and a report | `/do-it` sizes the work first. Small work skips the ceremony | | The agent builds something you did not mean | The plan is grilled with you and approved once, before any code. Each step is written as `step → verify:` | | The agent reviews its own work and finds nothing | Audit runs in fresh-context reviewers that see the plan and the diff, never the build transcript | | A long session loses the thread | State lives in a file, not the chat. `/clear` and resume any time | | A secret or a bad commit slips through | Hooks block secrets and env files before the edit and scan the diff before the commit | | The agent commits before you looked | Nothing is committed until you say "do it" at ship (a `--complete` run commits each verified phase locally; `--commit none` turns that off) | It does not own your process. Every step is also a skill you can call alone, and the plan, ADRs and context files are plain Markdown in your repo. ## What it looks like These sessions are condensed and illustrative; the wording varies. **A small fix (lane XS).** One file, no risk area: build, self-review, ship. ```text > /do-it #31 (issue: the 404 page says "Pagenotfound") Lane XS: one string in src/pages/NotFound.tsx, no risk area. [edits the string, runs the page's test, reads its own diff] Ship: commit "gh-31: fix 404 page title"? Say "do it", or leave it for review. ``` **A feature (lane S).** One approval on the plan, then it runs. ```text > /do-it "rate-limit the login endpoint" Lane S: auth is a risk area; `RateLimiter` exists in src/middleware/, only the login wiring is new. Plan (docs/planning/rate-limit-login.md) 1. Limit login to 5 tries per minute per IP → verify: 6th request returns 429 2. Reset the counter on success → verify: test passes Assumption: per IP, not per account. Approve? > yes [builds test-first; a fresh-context reviewer audits the diff against the plan] Audit PASS. 1 Nice: extract the limit to config. Ship: 1. keep all assumptions? 2. log the Nice as a to-do? 3. commit now or leave it? ``` **Picking it up tomorrow.** The state is in the plan file, so a new session starts where the old one stopped. ```text > /clear > /do-it rate-limit-login Resuming rate-limit-login: build is done and audited, waiting at ship. ``` **The guard.** An edit that writes a secret is refused before it lands, and the agent is told why. `DO_IT_HOOKS=off` turns the hooks off. **One-liners you will use** | Command | When | |---------|------| | `/do-it #42` or `/do-it ABC-123` | Work an issue from GitHub or Jira | | `/log-it "retry flaky upload"` | Park an idea or bug without planning it | | `/map-it payments` | Learn an unfamiliar area before changing it | | `/sweep-it --hot` | Audit the code that changes most for bugs and debt | | `/roadmap-it "move billing to Stripe"` | Chart work too big for one plan, then `/do-it docs/roadmap/billing.md#R1` | | `/do-it docs/roadmap/billing.md --complete` | Carry a whole roadmap to a reviewed finish: decisions settled up front, slices chained, stuck ones parked | | `/finish-it docs/roadmap/billing.md --resume` | Resume a run after you settled what parked a slice | | `/usage-it` | See what your sessions cost in tokens | ## Does it save tokens? Not by itself, and the docs should not claim it. do-it spends tokens to buy fewer wrong turns and less rework. Here is what is measured and what is not. | Question | Answer | Evidence | |----------|--------|----------| | What does it add to every session? | About 3,100 tokens: ~1,250 for the hook block (posture, project docs, code map), ~1,300 for skill descriptions, ~540 for the repo's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` | `usage.mjs --baseline` on this repo, against a median start context of about 53,600 tokens over 437 sessions | | Does small work stay cheap? | Lane XS skips the plan and the audit. A lane M run does more work than a bare prompt and costs more | By design; check your own with `/usage-it` | | Do the role agents cost less? | Scout runs on the cheap tier, builder and reviewer on the mid tier; only the planner and skeptic use the top tier. Pick one. **One-liner (Claude Code and OpenCode):** ```bash bash <(curl -fsSL 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rshingleton/do-it/main/scripts/install.sh') ``` It clones the repo into `~/.local/share/do-it` (or pulls it when the clone is there), then installs from the clone; re-run it to update. Options pass through: append `--no-hooks`, `--dry-run` or `--uninstall`. `DO_IT_REPO` points it at a mirror, `DO_IT_HOME` at another clone directory. **From a clone:** ```bash git clone https://github.com/rshingleton/do-it.git ~/.local/share/do-it cd ~/.local/share/do-it scripts/install.sh # skills, OpenCode commands and agents, hooks on scripts/install.sh --dry-run # show what it would do scripts/install.sh --no-hooks scripts/install.sh --uninstall ``` Skills link into `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills` (OpenCode reads both). The five role agents in `agents/` (`it-scout`, `it-reviewer`, `it-builder`, `it-planner`, `it-skeptic`) link into `~/.claude/agents`; each pins its own model, so skills that delegate pick the tier by naming the agent. For OpenCode, `.opencode/command/` (OpenCode 1) and `.opencode/commands/` (OpenCode 2) link into `~/.config/opencode/`, and `.opencode/agents/` links into `~/.config/opencode/agents/`: the same five roles, generated from `agents/` with a deny-first `permission` map in place of `tools` and no `model` (OpenCode has no tiers). Never link `agents/*.md` itself into an OpenCode agents directory: its `tools: Read, Grep` form makes OpenCode reject the whole config. An existing skill of the same name from another repo is skipped unless you pass `--force`. Hooks register in `~/.claude/settings.json` and `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`; each file is backed up as `*.bak-do-it` first. **Claude Code plugin:** ```text /plugin marketplace add rshingleton/do-it /plugin install do-it@do-it ``` The plugin carries skills, agents and hooks (its agents are namespaced, for example `do-it:it-reviewer`). Use it or the symlinks for Claude Code, not both. Using OpenCode too? Use the symlink install; it covers both hosts. **Update:** re-run the one-liner, `git pull` in the clone (symlinks pick it up), or `/plugin marketplace update do-it` for the plugin. ## Hooks On by default; `DO_IT_HOOKS=off` turns them off for a user, a repo or a shell. | When | Does | |------|------| | Session start, subagent start | Injects the `it-core` posture, pointers to the repo's standards and compliance rules, its resolved project docs, and a compact code map (`DO_IT_MAP=off` to skip) | | Before an edit | Blocks HIGH hits: secrets, env files, rules in `.compliance-rules/checks.json` | | After an edit | Reports MEDIUM/LOW hits; runs `DO_IT_LINT_CMD` on the file and feeds failures back | | Before `git commit` | Scans the staged diff and any untracked files the commit would add; blocks on HIGH. A `-m` message without an `: ` prefix gets a warning on Claude Code, never a block | | Session stop, subagent stop (Claude Code) | Records the run's token usage in a local ledger (see [Token usage](#token-usage)); suggests `/pass-it` then `/clear` when the context passes `DO_IT_CLEAR_AT` | Hooks fail open: a crash or bad input never blocks the agent, and a hook that runs long is cut off at its timeout. Mechanical rules (a regex decides) live in `checks.json` and run on every edit; judgement rules (`.compliance-rules/*.md`) are checked by `prove-it`. See [skills/guard-it/SKILL.md](skills/guard-it/SKILL.md). ### Code map The code map is capped at 1500 characters and takes the first source that exists: 1. The context map (`CONTEXT-MAP.md`): its headings and table rows, so a monorepo shows its areas and where each one's `CONTEXT.md` lives. Over budget it keeps the Context and Location columns before it drops rows. 2. The module map (`module-map.md` in the reference directory, written by `/map-it`): its first rows. 3. One `git ls-files` call (tracked and untracked files), capped at 1.5 seconds; on timeout the map is left out and nothing else changes. Monorepo `packages/`, `apps/` and `services/` show up to 12 packages each by name, and a top-level directory with its own manifest (`package.json`, `cpanfile`, `go.mod`, `pyproject.toml`, `Cargo.toml`) counts as a package. Packages come after shared code and before plain directories; `temp/`, `tmp/` and build output are skipped. It runs at every session and subagent start (every turn under OpenCode). `DO_IT_MAP=off` turns it off. ### OpenCode hooks OpenCode has no subagent-start hook; its plugin injects the posture into every turn's system prompt instead. The plugin's default export carries the OpenCode 1 hook object (`experimental.chat.system.transform`, `tool.execute.before/after`; a throw blocks the tool) and a v2 `setup` that registers `session` and `tool` hooks, which OpenCode 2 runs (verified on 2.1.2). Register the plugin as a directory on OpenCode 2 (`plugins`: `.opencode/plugins`, which holds an `index.js`); a plugin file path is skipped there. `scripts/install-hooks.mjs` picks the form from `opencode --version`. The OpenCode 2 `execute` code tool cannot write or run a command by itself on 2.1.2, and a nested tool call reaches the same guards. ### Token usage On Claude Code, the `Stop` and `SubagentStop` hooks sum each main session's and each subagent's tokens from its transcript and keep one line per run in `~/.claude/do-it/usage/.jsonl` (about 50 KB a heavy day) for 30 days (`DO_IT_USAGE_DAYS`). A line holds the tokens, the run's start and end times, and the context size of its first turn (`ctx0`) and its largest turn (`peak`). Older days roll up into `rollup.jsonl`, one row per day, agent, model and project, kept 365 days (`DO_IT_USAGE_ROLLUP_DAYS`) for trends. `DO_IT_USAGE_DIR` moves it all. Cost in dollars is not estimated, since prices change; tokens only. Days in every report are local calendar days; the files are named by UTC date. - `/usage-it` writes an HTML report: totals, work and cache reads over time, by agent, model and project, a context-outliers table (main sessions by peak context) and a plan-meter section. - `node skills/usage-it/scripts/usage.mjs [--days N, default 30 | --hours N] [--by agent|model|day|month|project] [--json]` prints the same rows as a table, rolled-up rows included (`--days 90 --by month` for a trend). `--from --to ` keeps runs that ended in that window, so a step's usage is its start and end time. `--import` first backfills from the transcripts Claude Code already keeps. `--baseline` prints what do-it adds to every session next to the median start context. - When a main session's context first passes `DO_IT_CLEAR_AT` tokens (default 300000, `0` is off), the `Stop` hook shows one line suggesting `/pass-it` then `/clear`. It never blocks and adds nothing to the model's context. - The plan meter: Claude Code caches its `/usage` percentages in `~/.claude.json`; the `Stop` hook and the report record each new reading, and the report charts the week, lists each day's growth and projects when the week would reach 100%. The report refreshes a stale cache first with `claude -p /usage` (no model call; `DO_IT_USAGE_REFRESH=0` turns it off) and re-imports the last two days of transcripts. `usage.mjs --snapshot` takes a reading now (or `--snapshot --week --resets ` gives one by hand). Readings are account-wide; the tokens stored with them are this host's. OpenCode notes for repos that use do-it: - OpenCode reads `AGENTS.md`, not `CLAUDE.md`. Put the standards in `AGENTS.md` (a `CLAUDE.md` that is only `@AGENTS.md` works for both hosts). - OpenCode 2 has no todo tool or LSP by default and allows `external_directory` by default; set it to `ask` or `deny` in `opencode.json` if the guards should not be sidestepped by paths outside the repo. `/setup-it` checks this and offers the fix. - The OpenCode plugin records the same token usage into the ledger (the `event` hook on 1.x, `ctx.event.subscribe` on 2.x), so `/usage-it` covers both hosts. description: Builds one approved plan phase on the mid tier, in a worktree when the brief names one, else in place. Use only when build-it names it for a phase.
model: sonnet
---

You build one phase of an approved plan and nothing else.

- Read the phase file and the plan README at the paths in the brief; the
  main session owns the state block, so read it and never write it.
- Read the `skills/test-it/SKILL.md` at the path in the brief and follow it;
  you cannot call a skill. Tests go only at the phase's `## Seams`.
- Work only in the worktree the brief names, and commit only on its scratch
  branch, as `build-it/PARALLEL.md` describes. No worktree named: work in
  place at the checkout root and never commit, stash or push.
- A failure you cannot fix in three rounds: report `failed`; main debugs.

## Report

Cap: 150 words, or the brief's lower cap.

- One line per edit: `path - what changed`.
- `verified:` the checks you ran and their result.
- Cannot go on: one token, then one line of why: `too-big` (phase will not
  fit), `needs-confirm` (an unknown only the user can settle), `ambiguous`
  (the phase reads two ways), `regressed` (a check that passed now fails).
- End with `done`, `blocked` or `failed` and one line.

## Voice for internal agent text

This format overrides any other style instruction.

Applies to text another agent or a script reads: briefs, reports, returns,
review findings, scout notes, state-block free text, script output, context
injected into subagents. It never
applies to replies or questions to the user, plans shown to the user,
closing messages, ADRs, README, docs, issues, commits or PR bodies; those stay
normal prose.

- Short sentences, one idea each. Drop articles and filler.
- Never drop "not", "never", "no" or "only". A lost negation costs more than
  every token saved.
- Numbers, paths, commands and errors stay verbatim.
- Plain wording wins when the terse form is not shorter.
- Full sentences for a security risk, a step that cannot be undone, and
  anything that needs the user to decide.
- Keep to the report shape and word cap the brief gives. No preamble, no
  recap, no restating the brief.
<!-- voice:end -->
