# Run commits

Only when a run record exists for the item (`work.mjs run show <slug>`, made
by `/do-it --complete`). No run record: none of this applies, and
[SKILL.md](SKILL.md) Rules hold (no commits). Why: ADR 0008.

## Mode

The record's `commit` value, set by `--commit phase|slice|none` and
defaulting to `phase`; `none` means build as usual and commit nothing.
`phase`: one commit per lane M phase. `slice`: one commit per slice; lane M
commits its code once, after its last phase verifies (no `--phase`, no tag),
then the closing docs.
`DO_IT_COMMIT=never` and the flag: see [CONFIG.md](../track-it/CONFIG.md).

## After a phase passes

1. `work.mjs verify-phase` (in a run, `work.mjs run verify`) must have passed
   for this phase (lane S: the item). A failed, skipped or stale verify never commits.
2. Run the commit boundary check in [STANDARDS.md](STANDARDS.md) §4 and keep
   the mapped file list.
3. `work.mjs run commit <slug> <id> --phase <n> --paths a,b` (lane S, or lane M
   in mode `slice`: no `--phase`; code changed since its last verify refuses).
   It picks the branch, stages those paths only, commits and, for a phase,
   tags `do-it/<id>/phase-<n>`.
   A lane M slice-mode commit needs the same mapped list given earlier to
   `work.mjs run verify <slug> <slice> --paths a,b`, which records only those
   files' hashes (never the user's or another slice's).
4. Closing docs (lane M after the last phase; lane S after its code commit):
   `work.mjs run commit <slug> <id> --docs --paths a,b`. Subject
   `<id>: closing docs`, no tag.
5. A check that could not run (no browser, no service): pass
   `--limits '["<what was not checked>"]'`. It goes in the run record and the
   commit body, never a trailer.

## What the script holds to

- Branch: the current one when unprotected (`main`, `master`,
  `DO_IT_PROTECTED_BRANCHES` are not), else `do-it/<roadmap-slug>`, made first.
- Message `<id>: phase <n> <title>` (lane S: `<id>: <title>`), then the single
  do-it line (the `ATTRIBUTION` constant in `commit.mjs`), and no other trailer.
- Never `git add -A` or `.`, a push, an amend or a force operation. Tags stay local.
- Staged files already in the index, or a path with no change: it stops and
  commits nothing.

# Build one phase in an agent

Keeps a phase's reads, edits and test output out of the main context. Main
sends one `it-builder` agent per phase and keeps only its short report.

## 1. The brief

Pointers, not pasted content:

- The absolute paths of the phase file, the plan README, `STANDARDS.md` and
  `skills/test-it/SKILL.md` (the agent cannot call a skill, so it reads it).
- The plan's `assumptions:`, and the cap: report under 150 words, naming any
  defect surfaced but not fixed.
- A worktree path when called from [PARALLEL.md](PARALLEL.md); none means
  in place at the checkout root, no commits.

## 2. What main does with the report

- `done`: `work.mjs verify-phase <id> <n> --brief -- "<commands>"` (in a run,
  `work.mjs run verify`). Main owns
  every state-block write.
- `failed`: main may call the Skill tool with "debug-it" itself, then send
  the phase once more; a second `failed` is `blocked`.
- Anything else (`blocked`, `too-big`, `needs-confirm`, `ambiguous`,
  `regressed`): `work.mjs event <id> block "<why>" --phase <n>` and stop.
  Other phases that do not depend on it keep going.

## 3. When main builds instead

Lane S, fix mode, a host without subagents, or the user said to build in
main. Then follow §3 of [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) in the main context.

## 4. One at a time

Never start an agent beside other in-place work: two in the same checkout
would edit the same tree. Parallel phases get worktrees per PARALLEL.md.

# Parallel phases without committing on the user's branch

Phases run in their own worktrees on scratch branches, merge into a scratch
integration branch, and land on the user's branch as one uncommitted change.
The scratch commits never reach the user's branch.

## Preconditions

- More than one frontier phase.
- The user's tree has no uncommitted changes outside `docs/planning/`. If
  earlier phases were built in place, build the rest in place too.
- The host can run background subagents. Otherwise build sequentially.

## 1. Scratch integration branch

```bash
top=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
# Absolute, so every later git -C and worktree command resolves it the same way.
root="$(dirname "$top")/$(basename "$top").do-it/<id>"
git worktree add "$root/int" -b "do-it/<id>" <base_ref>
```

The planning files stay only in the user's checkout. Implementers read them
there by absolute path, so the scratch branches carry code alone and the final
squash cannot collide with the uncommitted plan.

## 2. One implementer per frontier phase

```bash
git worktree add "$root/phase-N" -b "do-it/<id>--phase-N" "do-it/<id>"
```

Start one background `it-builder` agent per phase, briefed per
[DELEGATE.md](DELEGATE.md) §1 (report under 150 words) with its worktree
path. Add to the brief:

1. Commit everything in the worktree as `<id> phase-N (scratch)`.
2. Report `done | blocked | failed`, the commands that passed, new
   assumptions, surfaced defects, and anything blocking. Not the transcript.

## 3. Merge one at a time

For each finished phase, in `$root/int`:

```bash
git merge --no-ff "do-it/<id>--phase-N" -m "<id> phase-N (scratch)"
```

On a conflict, call the Skill tool with "merge-it", passing the plan path so
it resolves by the plan's intent.

Then, from the user's checkout, run the project's checks in `int` through
the gate, which records the phase only when they exit 0:

```bash
work.mjs verify-phase <id> <n> --in "$root/int" -- "<checks>"
```

In a complete run use `work.mjs run verify <slug> <slice> --phase <n> --in ...`.

On a failed check, `git reset --hard HEAD~1` in the scratch worktree only,
`work.mjs event <id> block "<why>" --phase <n>`, and keep going with phases
that do not depend on it. Otherwise recompute the frontier and start
implementers for newly ready phases.

## 4. Land and clean up

When no phase can start, from the user's checkout:

```bash
git merge --squash "do-it/<id>"     # stages the change; commits nothing
git reset -q                        # unstage, so the user reviews a plain working tree
git worktree remove "$root/phase-N" # each phase worktree
git worktree remove "$root/int"
git branch -D "do-it/<id>" "do-it/<id>--phase-N"
```

Leave a blocked phase's branch and worktree in place and name them in
the report.

# Probing

Stage 4 of [debug-it](SKILL.md).

## Order of tools

1. A debugger or REPL, where the environment allows it: one paused frame shows
   more than a page of output.
2. A few log lines at the boundaries that tell the hypotheses apart.
3. Never blanket logging followed by a search through the noise.

## Tag every probe

Give every temporary log or print one unique tag for this session, such as
`[dbg-7c1e]`. At the end a single grep for the tag finds every probe, so none
ship. Untagged debug output is how stray prints reach production.

## Slowness is measured, not logged

For a performance regression, logs mislead. Take a baseline first (a timing
harness, `performance.now()`, a profiler, the database's query plan), then
bisect or vary one thing at a time against that number. No fix before a
measurement says where the time goes.

# Building the loop

Stage 1 of [debug-it](SKILL.md). Try these roughly in order; earlier ones are
cheaper and sharper.

| # | Loop | Fits when |
|---|------|-----------|
| 1 | A failing test at the nearest seam that reaches the bug | Almost always; start here |
| 2 | A scripted HTTP call against a local server | The symptom is a response |
| 3 | The CLI run on a fixture, output diffed against a known-good copy | The symptom is output |
| 4 | A headless browser script asserting on the page, console or network | The symptom is in the UI |
| 5 | A captured request, payload or event replayed through the code alone | The bug came from real traffic |
| 6 | A minimal harness: one service, faked neighbours, one call | The full system is too heavy to run |
| 7 | Many random inputs, checking a property | The output is only sometimes wrong |
| 8 | `git bisect run` over a check script | It worked at some earlier commit, version or dataset |
| 9 | The same input through two versions or configs, outputs diffed | Something

it tighter

Once a loop exists, improve it like a product:

- **Faster:** cache setup, skip unrelated start-up, narrow the test scope.
- **Sharper:** assert on the exact symptom, never just "did not crash".
- **Steadier:** freeze the clock, seed randomness, isolate the file system,
  stub the network.

A two-second loop that always gives the same answer is worth far more than a
thirty-second loop that sometimes does.

## Intermittent bugs

Aim for a higher failure rate, not a perfect repro. Run the trigger hundreds
of times, in parallel, under load, with sleeps or yields inserted to widen
the timing window. Half the runs failing is workable; one in a hundred is
not yet, so keep raising it.

## When no loop is possible

Say so plainly and list what was tried. Then ask for one of: access to an
environment where it happens; a redacted artifact (HAR file, logs, core dump,
a timestamped screen recording); or permission to add temporary
instrumentation where it happens. Do not move on to hypotheses without a
loop.

# Deepening safely

How to merge a cluster of shallow modules into one deeper module, and where
its tests go. Terms are from [SKILL.md](SKILL.md).

## Sort the dependencies first

What the cluster depends on decides how the deepened module is tested at its
seam. Classify each dependency:

| Kind | Examples | How to deepen and test |
|------|----------|------------------------|
| **In-process** | pure functions, in-memory state | Merge freely. Test through the new interface; no adapter needed. |
| **Local stand-in exists** | an embedded or in-memory version of the database, a temp filesystem | Merge, and run the stand-in inside the test suite. The seam stays internal; the module's interface does not change for it. |
| **Owned, over the network** | your own services and internal APIs | Put an interface at the seam. The logic lives in the deep module; the transport is an adapter (HTTP or queue in production, in-memory in tests). |
| **Third party** | payment, messaging or mail providers | The module receives the provider through an interface; tests pass a fake adapter. |

A typical recommendation for the third row: "Put an interface where the
service call is, keep the logic in one module, and give it an HTTP adapter
for production and an in-memory one for tests."

## Seams

- Add an interface at a seam only when at least two adapters will use it,
  usually production and test. A single adapter is just indirection.
- A deep module can keep internal seams for its own tests. Do not widen its
  interface to expose them.

## Tests move, they do not pile up

- Write the new tests at the deepened module's interface; that is the test
  surface now.
- Delete the old tests that pinned the shallow pieces once the new ones cover
  the behaviour. Keeping both doubles the cost of every change.
- Assert what a caller can observe, never internal state. A test that breaks
  when only the inside changes was testing past the interface.

# Designing an interface more than once

The first interface you think of is rarely the best. When a candidate is
chosen (from `deepen-it`, or a seam `scope-it` is unsure about), design it
several ways in parallel and compare. Terms are from [SKILL.md](SKILL.md).

## 1. Lay out the problem for the user

Before starting any subagent, write the user a short account of:

- what any interface here must satisfy (callers, invariants, failure cases);
- what it depends on, sorted by kind as in [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md);
- a rough code sketch that makes those constraints concrete. It illustrates
  the problem; it is not a proposal.

Send it and carry straight on; the user reads while the designs are drawn.

## 2. Draw three or more designs at once

Start at least three subagents together, on the session model (the designs are
the thinking this skill exists for), each reporting under 500 words. Each gets
the same technical brief (file paths, how the pieces are coupled, the
dependency kinds, what must sit behind the seam, the `design-it` terms and the
Terms in the area's `CONTEXT.md`) and one different pull:

| Designer | Pull |
|----------|------|
| A | The fewest entry points that still serve every caller. |
| B | Room to grow: many uses, extension without edits. |
| C | The most common call is a one-liner; rare cases may cost more. |
| D (when dependencies cross the network) | Interfaces and adapters at every outside dependency. |

Each returns:

1. the interface: signatures plus invariants, call order and failure modes;
2. a caller using it;
3. what the implementation hides behind the seam;
4. which dependencies get adapters, and which adapters;
5. where it gives the most leverage and where it is thin.

## 3. Compare and recommend

Show the designs one after another, then compare them on depth, locality and
where each puts the seam. Finish with a recommendation: the design you would
build and why, or a combination of parts from two of them. Give a firm view;
the user can overrule it.

# Shaping an interface

Detail for [design-it](SKILL.md).

## Deep and shallow at a glance

```text
deep                              shallow
+-----------+                     +-----------------------------+
| narrow    |  few entry points   | wide                        |  many entry points,
+-----------+                     +-----------------------------+  many parameters
|           |                     | thin: mostly forwards calls |
|  a lot of |  behaviour hidden   +-----------------------------+
|  behaviour|
|           |
+-----------+
```

## Making it smaller

For each entry point, ask:

- Could two entry points become one, with the difference handled inside?
- Could a parameter be derived, defaulted, or moved into construction?
- Is the caller doing work (ordering calls, checking state, retrying) the
  module could do for it?

Each "yes" moves complexity behind the interface, where it is paid for once.

## Shaping it for tests

An interface that is easy to test is usually easy to call. Three habits get
most of the way there:

1. **Take collaborators in, do not build them inside.** A module that
   receives its clock, store or gateway can be tested with fakes at that
   seam:

   ```python
   # testable: the gateway arrives from outside
   def settle(invoice, gateway): ...

   # hard to test: the gateway is created inside
   def settle(invoice):
       gateway = CardGateway(api_key=load_key())
   ```

2. **Return a result instead of changing things in place.** A returned value
   can be asserted directly; a mutation has to be observed somewhere else:

   ```python
   # testable
   def price_with_discount(basket) -> Price: ...

   # harder: the effect hides inside the argument
   def apply_discount(basket) -> None: ...
   ```

3. **Keep the surface small.** Fewer entry points need fewer tests; fewer
   parameters need less setup per test.

# Between steps

Each step hands off through the state block, so the conversation is never
the record. Decide what to do with the context only at a step boundary,
never in the middle of a step.

| At the boundary | Do |
|-----------------|----|
| Lane XS or S, context still small | Continue in the same session |
| Plan approved on lane M (the grill filled the context) | Suggest a fresh session: the user clears, then runs `/do-it <id>`; build starts from the plan alone |
| Between M phases built in place, context getting long | Same: fresh session, `/do-it <id>` resumes from the frontier |
| Lane M build done, before the audit; or any step with the context past about 100k tokens | Same: fresh session, `/do-it <id>` resumes at `prove-it`. The reviewers start cold from pointers, so nothing in this conversation is needed |
| Switching agent or host (Claude Code to OpenCode, or another person) | Follow [pass-it](../pass-it/SKILL.md): it points at the work item instead of restating it |
| Audit | Nothing to do: prove-it's reviewers already run in fresh subagents |

Rules:

- Suggest, do not force: one line in the closing message, e.g. "Plan
  approved. A fresh session keeps the build focused: clear, then
  `/do-it login-rate-limit`."
- Before suggesting a fresh session, make sure the state block holds
  everything the next step needs (approvals, assumptions, blocker).
- Compaction is the last resort: it keeps a summary of the conversation, not
  the plan. Prefer a fresh session that reads the plan.

# Levels

The record's `level` (`work.mjs run show <slug>`). One branch each; the loop
in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) is the same.

## lite

Decisions are still settled up front, but the run keeps a human gate per
slice. Scope-it follows its normal grill, not the non-interactive form. Ship-it
asks its one question and the commit question as it does outside a run. After
each slice, close per SKILL.md §4 with the slice shipped; the user resumes with
`/finish-it <file>` for the next one.

## full (default)

Chain every slice that can go on. Scope-it is non-interactive, ship-it runs in
[run mode](../ship-it/RUNMODE.md), and commits follow the record's `commit`.
One close, when `run next` returns no slice.

## ultra

Everything in `full`. The up-front sweep also challenges each slice the
destination does not justify, per [SWEEP.md](../roadmap-it/SWEEP.md) §3. The
run itself pushes back no further: a slice the user kept is built.

# Stops

Every reason a run parks a slice or stops. Codes match
`skills/do-it/scripts/stops.mjs`; a test compares the two. A parked slice
waits with its dependents and the run goes on. A stop ends the loop and
closes per [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) §4.

## Gates (the script decides)

Before chaining a slice to ship, `work.mjs run gate <slug> <slice>` prints
`{allow, reason, detail}`. `allow` false: act on `reason`.

- `STALE_VERIFY` (park): code changed since the last passing verify. Rerun `work.mjs run verify`.
- `UNVERIFIED` (park): no passing verify recorded. Run `work.mjs run verify`.

## Voice for internal agent text

This format overrides any other style instruction.

Applies to text another agent or a script reads: briefs, reports, returns,
review findings, scout notes, state-block free text, script output, context
injected into subagents. It never
applies to replies or questions to the user, plans shown to the user,
closing messages, ADRs, README, docs, issues, commits or PR bodies; those stay
normal prose.

- Short sentences, one idea each. Drop articles and filler.
- Never drop "not", "never", "no" or "only". A lost negation costs more than
  every token saved.
- Numbers, paths, commands and errors stay verbatim.
- Plain wording wins when the terse form is not shorter.
- Full sentences for a security risk, a step that cannot be undone, and
  anything that needs the user to decide.
- Keep to the report shape and word cap the brief gives. No preamble, no
  recap, no restating the brief.

# Validating Must findings

A reviewer that found a problem is the worst judge of whether it is real. Before
a **Must** counts, a fresh `it-reviewer` agent (mid-tier model) tries to
confirm it from the code alone. Should and Nice findings skip this step: they never block.

## Who gets what

One validator (an `it-reviewer` agent, mid-tier model) per batch of up to
five Musts. For each finding it gets only:

- the claim, in one sentence ("`settle()` charges twice when the gateway times
  out");
- the concrete case the finding named (file and line, input, or scenario);
- pointers: the diff command, the files involved, the plan path when the
  finding is about the spec.

Never the reviewer's reasoning, the other findings' text, or the build
conversation. The validator starts cold on purpose.

## The brief

> For each claim, check the code yourself. Confirm it only if you can show it:
> the lines that cause it, the input or state that triggers it, and what goes
> wrong. Reject it if the code does not do what the claim says, if the case
> cannot happen (a guard, a type, a caller that never passes it), if a
> recorded decision in the plan or an ADR covers it, or if a linter already
> catches it. One line per claim: `confirmed | file:line | evidence` or
> `rejected | reason`. Under 40 words a line.

## Using the answers

- `confirmed`: the finding stays a Must, with the validator's evidence added to
  its case.
- `rejected`: the finding is dropped from the Must group and listed under
  **Not confirmed** in the report with the validator's reason, so the user can
  overrule it. It does not block.
- A failed mechanical check (a test, lint or type-check command that exited
  non-zero) needs no validator: the command output is the evidence.

Every audit round validates its Musts afresh; a confirmation from an earlier
round does not carry over.

# Fit and hygiene baseline

Checked by the Standards reviewer alongside [SMELLS.md](SMELLS.md), in a repo
that documents nothing as much as in one that documents everything. A
documented repo rule overrides any line here. Skip what tooling enforces.

Not here on purpose, because each has one home elsewhere: minimal surface and
surgical changes (the it-core posture), dependency policy (guard-it),
`shortcut:` markers as recorded decisions (prove-it's report contract),
module depth and seams (design-it).

## Fit

- **Match the surroundings.** Names, imports, layout, error handling and
  comment density look like the code next to them.
- **Comments say why.** A comment earns its place by explaining a non-obvious
  reason; one that repeats what the code says is noise.

## Hygiene

- UTF-8 text, LF line endings unless `.gitattributes` says otherwise.
- Shell scripts executable; other files not.
- A copyright or licence header on new files where their siblings carry one.

# Smell baseline

The Standards reviewer checks these even in a repo that documents nothing.
They come from the code-smell catalogue in Martin Fowler's _Refactoring_.
Each is a hint worth a look, reported as "possible <smell>", never as a rule
broken. A documented repo rule that allows the pattern switches the smell off.

| Smell | Looks like, in a diff | Usual remedy |
|-------|-----------------------|--------------|
| Unclear name | A name that does not say what the thing holds or does | Rename; if no honest name comes, the design needs another look |
| Repeated logic | The same shape of code in two hunks or files of this change | One shared function both call |
| Envy | A function busier with another object's fields than its own | Move it next to the data it uses |
| Travelling group | The same few values passed together again and again | Make them one type |
| Bare primitive | A string or number standing in for a domain idea | A small type of its own |
| Repeated branching | The same switch or if-chain on the same kind recurring | One lookup or polymorphism shared by both sites |
| Scattered edit | One logical change touching many files | Gather what changes together into one module |
| Mixed reasons | One file edited for several unrelated reasons | Split it along those reasons |
| Just-in-case | Parameters, hooks or layers the spec never asked for | Delete; add back when a real need shows up |
| Long chains | `a.b().c().d()` walks the caller should not know about | One method on the first object hides the walk |
| Pass-through | A class or function that only hands calls onward | Remove it and call the real target (the deletion test in [design-it](../design-it/SKILL.md) confirms it) |
| Ignored inheritance | A subclass that overrides or ignores most of its parent | Composition instead of inheritance |

# Slicing a roadmap

A good slice is a thin path through every layer it touches that ships on its
own and leaves the product better or the next slice easier. A good roadmap is
mostly slices like that, a few spikes, and an honest list of what is not yet
known.

## Kinds of slice

| Kind | Use when | Verify |
|------|----------|--------|
| **Build** | The behaviour is clear enough to plan | Its Verify check passes in the shipped product |
| **Spike** | A question blocks planning and only trying will answer it (performance, a vendor API, a UX doubt) | The question is answered, recorded as a decision or an ADR, and the throwaway code is gone (sketch-it) |
| **Enabler** | A refactor or platform piece that several slices need | The slices that depend on it can start; nothing user-visible is required |

Prefer build slices. An enabler with no slice depending on it is not a slice.

## Cutting rules

- **Vertical, not layered.** "Search returns results from the new index" is
  a slice; "build the index schema" alone i
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
Expand, migrate, contract** for wide changes: add the new form beside the
  old, move users over in batches, then remove the old form, each its own
  slice.

## Not slices

- **Open decisions:** a question you can state sharply now but not answer
  yet. Each names how it gets answered (grill, look-it-up, spike) and which
  slices wait on it.
- **Fog:** areas you know are coming but cannot phrase sharply yet. Coarser
  than a slice; a patch of fog may become several slices or none.
- **Out of scope:** beyond the destination. Never graduates; it returns only
  as a new roadmap.

## Checks before approval (and after every replan)

- Every requirement (`G`) is covered by a slice, sits in Fog, or is in Out
  of scope. None is silently missing.
- No cycle in Blocked by, and no block that only restates order.
- Every milestone has an exit check, and the first one proves the path end
  to end.
- Every slice fits lane S or M and has a Verify.
- Every open decision says how it gets answered and which slices it blocks.

# Greenfield agenda (new project)

A new project has no code to read, so its first plan decides what the code
will look like. Add these branches to the grill; for lane S, ask only the ones
the request leaves open.

## Decide

- **Purpose and first user.** The one job the first release must do, and for
  whom. Everything else is a non-goal for now.
- **Stack and runtime.** Language, framework, package manager, where it runs.
  Check org standards first: `AGENTS.md`, `.compliance-rules/`, a sibling
  repo the user names. Facts about a library or platform go to the `look-it-up`
  skill, not guesses.
- **Shape.** The first few modules and their seams, in the `design-it`
  vocabulary. Prefer one deep module over several shallow ones until a second
  adapter is real.
- **Data and integrations.** What is stored, what is called, what is secret.
- **Quality bar.** Test runner and levels, lint, format, type-check, CI.

## Record

Foundation choices usually pass all three ADR tests (hard to reverse,
surprising without context, a real trade-off): stack, persistence, deployment
shape. Write those as ADRs. Do not ADR defaults nobody would question.

## Phases

1. **Walking skeleton.** The thinnest end-to-end path: one entry point, one
   test, the build, lint and test commands working, CI running them. Ends with
   `AGENTS.md` naming those commands and the layout, `.do-it/config.env` for
   the tracker and lint command, and `.gitignore`.
2. **First vertical slice** of the purpose above, test-first at its seams.
3. Further slices as the grill found them.

The skeleton phase blocks every other phase. Its `→ verify:` is the commands
running green from a clean checkout.

# Grill agenda (lane M)

Add these branches to the `grill-it` design tree:

- **One plan or several.** Merge overlapping issues; split work that ships
  independently. A split into several shippable efforts means lane L: a
  roadmap (roadmap-it) instead of one plan.
- **Vertical slices.** Each phase is a narrow path through every layer it
  touches, verifiable on its own, and fits one fresh context window.
  Prefactoring goes first, in its own phase if it is more than trivial.
- **Wide mechanical refactors** are the exception: expand (add the new form
  beside the old), migrate call sites in batches each blocked by the expand,
  contract (delete the old form) blocked by every batch.
- **Blocking edges.** For each phase, the phases that must finish first.
- **Seams.** For each phase, the public interfaces tests will sit at, what a
  test there catches and what it misses. A phase with no code seam names its
  observable check instead.
- **Assumptions.** Reversible defaults the build may take without asking.
- **Deferred decisions and risk.**

When the open branches are down to confirmations, write the plan and run its
checks (scope-it §3) before asking again. That last round is the plan
approval: the phases with `Blocked by`, the assumptions and any builder
questions, in one turn. The user's "do it" approves both; there is no separate
approval stop.

# Non-interactive scope-it (complete runs)

Used when a run record exists for the slice's roadmap
(`docs/planning/<roadmap-slug>.run/RUN.md`, `work.mjs run show <slug>`) and its
level is `full` or `ultra`. At `lite` follow the normal grill instead. The up-front
sweep ([SWEEP.md](../roadmap-it/SWEEP.md)) already settled the decisions, so this
plan asks no question and ends no turn for an answer.

## Steps

1. Skip the grill. Read the roadmap's `Decisions so far` and the run record's
   `assumptions`; treat each as an answer.
2. Scout the code and ADRs for the rest, as in the normal path.
3. A new unknown, sorted by it-core's assume-or-ask:
   - Reversible and low impact: decide it, add it to the plan's `assumptions:`
     and to the run record (`work.mjs run add-assumptions <slug> <id> '<json>'`), with a
     stop-if-wrong note.
   - Fails assume-or-ask (irreversible, scope, money, credentials, data loss),
     or is an `ask-when-reached` decision: do not ask. Park the slice with
     `work.mjs run slice <slug> <id> parked --needs decision --reason "<the question>"`
     and return `blocked`.
4. Write the plan and run [CHECKS.md](CHECKS.md). Builder-check questions that
   need the user park the slice the same way; the rest are fixed or assumed.
5. Approve the plan yourself: the roadmap approval covered it. Run

# Lenses

Look through each lens at the scope. Order of importance: correct, safe,
holds under the expected load, tested, fast, lean.

## Correctness and risk

1. **Bug.** Wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
   rounding, time zones, encoding); callers that disagree with what a
   function returns; the same rule implemented differently in two places.
2. **Risk.** Injection, missing checks on user input, weak randomness,
   secrets in code, authorization gaps; data loss through swallowed errors,
   writes in the wrong order, missing transactions.
3. **Scale.** Fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, a
   query per item, memory or lists that only grow, per-process state that
   must be shared, O(n²) on real input sizes.

## Tests

4. **Test gap.** Risky logic (a branch, a parser, money, auth, data writes)
   with no test that would fail if it broke. Flaky, skipped or
   environment-dependent suites. Recommend one good test per gap, at the

# do-it configuration

Dotenv files (`KEY=value`, `#` comments, optional quotes, no interpolation),
read in this order; later wins:

| # | File | Holds | Commit it? |
|---|------|-------|------------|
| 1 | built-in defaults | | |
| 2 | `~/.config/do-it/config.env` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) | Your defaults for every repo, and secrets | n/a (`chmod 600`) |

| 4 | `<repo>/.do-it/local.env` | Your overrides and secrets for this repo | No (gitignore it) |
| 5 | Environment variables `DO_IT_*`, `JIRA_*`, `GITHUB_*` | One-off overrides, CI | n/a |

warns when a token-like key sits in the committed project file.
